statement: Many governments spend large amounts of public money on major projects such as high-speed railways, new airports and national stadiums, while local services such as libraries and youth centres are being closed.
question: Why do governments choose to fund large projects? Do you think this is the right priority?
model:
Ribbon-cutting ceremonies at gleaming new airports make for impressive news coverage, whereas the quiet closure of a branch library rarely attracts attention. This contrast helps to explain why governments favour grand projects, but in my view the balance has tipped too far against the local services on which communities depend.

There are several reasons why large schemes are so attractive to those in power. Some are economically justified: a high-speed railway can shorten journey times between cities, encourage investment in neglected regions and provide thousands of construction jobs. Major infrastructure also signals national ambition and can raise a country's international profile, as the stadiums built for events such as the Olympic Games are intended to do. However, political motives play a significant role as well. A new airport is a visible, lasting monument that a minister can point to at the next election, while the benefits of a youth centre, such as a teenager who avoids crime or a pensioner who escapes loneliness, are real but almost impossible to photograph.

I would argue that this preference is often misguided. Large projects frequently run far over budget; Britain's HS2 railway, for instance, has seen its estimated cost multiply while parts of the route have been cancelled. Meanwhile, modest sums could keep dozens of libraries open, providing free internet access, homework support and warm, safe spaces for people who have nowhere else to go. Cutting such services may save money in the short term, but it frequently creates greater costs later, through higher demand on health care, policing and social services.

In conclusion, governments favour major projects because they promise economic growth and political prestige. While some infrastructure is undoubtedly necessary, I believe that maintaining everyday local services should take priority, since their benefits reach far more citizens directly.
